title: Pyu City-States
capsule: The Pyu were an early Tibeto-Burman-speaking civilization occupying the Irrawaddy valley in present-day Myanmar from at least the first century CE, organized as a network of walled urban centers rather than a centralized empire, with major cities including Beikthano, Halin (664 hectares), and Sri Ksetra (~1,400 hectares). The Pyu adopted Theravada Buddhism by the fourth century CE and developed a Brahmi-derived script that influenced later Burmese writing, while maintaining trade links with China and India documented in Chinese dynastic histories. In 832 CE, Nanzhao kingdom raiders carried off some 3,000 Pyu captives from Halin, a blow from which the northern cities did not recover; Sri Ksetra persisted longer but the Pyu were gradually absorbed as Pagan consolidated the Irrawaddy valley in the eleventh century. The Pyu script was deciphered in the nineteenth century and Pyu sites were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Individual Pyu cities are well-attested archaeologically and in Tang dynasty Chinese records, but the political boundaries between city-states and their combined territorial extent are not documented and must be estimated from settlement distributions.
